title: The Units That Reported More Errors
text:
In the early 1990s Amy Edmondson, then a doctoral student at Harvard, joined a large study of medication errors in hospitals. Her task was to look at the nursing units involved and see whether the quality of their teamwork and leadership affected how many drug errors they made. She surveyed the staff of eight units in two hospitals, while medical researchers independently tracked the errors.

The data showed something unexpected. The units with the best leadership and the strongest working relationships did not have fewer errors. They appeared to have more. At first Edmondson thought the analysis was wrong. Then she considered a different explanation: perhaps the better units were not making more mistakes, but were more willing to report them.

To find out, a research assistant who did not know her hypothesis visited the units and observed how they worked. In some units, nurses said that mistakes were natural and talked about them openly. In others, nurses described being treated as if on trial when an error came to light, and admitting a mistake felt dangerous. The units where it felt safe to speak up were the ones with the higher reported error rates. The insight became the basis of Edmondson's later work on psychological safety.
lesson: A low count of reported problems may mean people are hiding them. Leaders who make it safe to admit mistakes see their problems early enough to fix them.
source: Edmondson, A. C. (1996). Learning from mistakes is easier said than done: Group and organizational influences on the detection and correction of human error. Journal of Applied Behavioral Science, 32(1), 5-28.
